3.1.title: SNMP Versions — v1 vs v2c vs v3
rows: Original standard; GetRequest, SetRequest, GetNextRequest, Trap
Common but insecure — community strings cleartext
AuthNoPriv (auth+no encrypt), AuthPriv (auth+encrypt with AES/DES), NoAuthNoPriv
key_points: SNMPv1/v2c: community string 'public' = read-only, 'private' = read-write. Both cleartext — sniffable.
SNMPv3 AuthPriv mode: authentication (MD5/SHA) + encryption (AES/DES). Use this for production.
SNMP uses UDP 161 for queries (manager → agent), UDP 162 for traps/informs (agent → manager).
Trap = unreliable (fire-and-forget). Inform = reliable (agent retransmits until ACK).
MIB (Management Information Base): database of manageable objects on a device.
OID (Object Identifier): unique numeric address for each MIB object (e.g., 1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1 = sysDescr).

3.1.title: Syslog Severity Levels
rows: Database corruption, loss of backup primary
Disk space low, config change warning
User login, config saved, service started
key_points: Mnemonic: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Daily Biscuits (0-7).
Lower number = higher severity. 0 is worst, 7 is most verbose.
Syslog uses UDP 514 (default) or TCP 514/6514 (TLS-secured).
Syslog server (collector): centralised log aggregation — Graylog, Splunk, syslog-ng.
Severity 0-3: critical/alerts requiring immediate attention.
Production devices usually set to level 5 (Notice) or 6 (Info) — level 7 (Debug) floods logs.

3.1.title: Network Monitoring Tools Comparison
rows: Device health: CPU, memory, interface counters, config
Traffic flows: src/dst IP, port, protocol, bytes
Bandwidth analysis, traffic patterns, anomaly detection
Network traffic stats captured at remote devices
Detailed traffic analysis without centralised polling
Full packet capture from a switch port
Packet analysis with Wireshark; IDS sensors
key_points: NetFlow = flow-level visibility (who talked to whom, how much). SNMP = device-level stats.
SPAN (Switched Port Analyzer) / port mirroring: copies traffic from source port to monitor port for analysis.
RSPAN (Remote SPAN): mirrors traffic across the network to a remote switch port.
Baseline: record normal performance metrics to compare against anomalies later.
NMS (Network Management System): software platform that uses SNMP to monitor/manage all devices.
Nagios, PRTG, SolarWinds, Zabbix — common NMS platforms.

3.2.title: Network Performance Metrics
rows: Maximum data transfer capacity of a link
Lower than expected = overhead, errors, congestion
Time for a packet to travel from source to destination
Variation in latency between consecutive packets
Percentage of packets that fail to reach destination
key_points: VoIP quality thresholds: latency <150ms, jitter <30ms, packet loss <1%.
Bandwidth ≠ throughput. Bandwidth is the pipe size; throughput is actual water flowing.
Jitter buffer: VoIP devices use a small buffer to smooth out jitter — too large = latency, too small = choppy.
Packet loss causes TCP to trigger congestion control (slow start) — dramatically reduces throughput.
Establish a BASELINE of normal metrics — anomaly detection compares current vs baseline.

3.2.title: QoS — Differentiated Services & Queuing
rows: Marks IP packets for priority treatment. EF=46 (VoIP), AF classes, CS classes, BE=0 (default)
VLAN-tagged frames only. 7=highest priority. Mapped to DSCP at L3 boundary.
Buffers excess traffic — introduces delay but avoids drops
Drops or re-marks excess traffic immediately — no buffering
Guarantees VoIP/real-time traffic is always served first
Assigns minimum bandwidth guarantee per traffic class
key_points: DSCP EF (Expedited Forwarding) = 46 — used for VoIP/real-time traffic (strict priority).
DSCP BE (Best Effort) = 0 — default, no special treatment.
Shaping vs Policing: shaping queues excess (smooth, adds delay). Policing drops excess (harsh, immediate).
QoS must be configured end-to-end — a single device without QoS breaks the chain.
Voice traffic: mark at ingress (access port), trust DSCP at core, use LLQ for guaranteed forwarding.

3.2.title: Interface Errors & Diagnostics
rows: Frames < 64 bytes — collision or malformed frames
Check for collisions, duplex mismatch, or faulty NIC
Check for jumbo frame misconfiguration or MTU mismatch
Corrupt frames — bad cable, connector, or interference
Replace cable, check SFP/connector, test cable with tester
Drops due to buffer overflow or hardware issues
Check interface utilisation — possible upgrade needed
One end full-duplex, other half-duplex → collisions and errors
Set both ends to same duplex explicitly — disable auto-negotiate
Check cable, SFP, remote port, or spanning tree issue
key_points: Duplex mismatch: most common cause of CRC errors + late collisions on Ethernet links.
Auto-negotiate: can fail — best practice is explicit speed/duplex on server and uplink ports.
Late collisions (detected >512 bits into frame) = strong indicator of duplex mismatch.
show interface: key command to see all error counters on Cisco devices.
Runts + collisions together = typical half-duplex or duplex mismatch scenario.

3.3.title: Network Diagram Types
rows: Network topology, IP addressing, VLANs, routing
IP subnets, routers, switches, VLANs, cloud symbols
Troubleshooting, capacity planning, understanding traffic flow
Actual physical layout of equipment and connections
Exact device locations, cable types, port numbers
Cable runs, patch panel mappings, port-to-port
Cable IDs, patch panel labels, wall jack locations
Rack unit layout — what's installed where in each rack
Device model, U position, PDU, cable management
Traffic flows, bandwidth utilization at normal operation
key_points: Logical ≠ Physical: two devices can be adjacent logically but floors apart physically.
Documentation is a living document — update after every change.
IP address management (IPAM): software or spreadsheet tracking all assigned IPs, subnets, DNS.
Out-of-date documentation is worse than no documentation — it misleads troubleshooting.
Rack diagram should include power draw (W per device) to prevent PDU/UPS overload.

3.3.title: Change Management Process
3.3.body:
Change management ensures network changes are planned, reviewed, and reversible — reducing outages from uncontrolled changes.

KEY STEPS:
  1. RFC (Request for Change): document the change, reason, scope, schedule, rollback plan
  2. CAB (Change Advisory Board): reviews and approves/rejects the RFC
  3. Change window: scheduled maintenance period (often low-traffic hours)
  4. Implementation: execute the change following the documented procedure
  5. Testing: verify the change works as expected
  6. Rollback: revert using the documented rollback plan if something breaks
  7. Documentation update: update diagrams, IP docs, configs after successful change

CHANGE TYPES:
  • Standard change: pre-approved, low risk, recurring (e.g., adding a user)
  • Normal change: requires RFC + CAB approval
  • Emergency change: expedited process for critical issues (post-change documentation still required)
key_points: Every change needs a rollback plan — know how to undo it before you start.
Change window: schedule during low-impact hours (nights/weekends for business networks).
CAB (Change Advisory Board): committee that evaluates risk and approves changes.
Emergency changes: still document after the fact — 'fix first, document second'.
Configuration backups: always back up device config BEFORE making changes.
RFC must include: reason, scope, risk assessment, test plan, rollback plan, schedule.

3.3.title: Policies and Agreements
rows: Defines permitted use of org network/systems
Users must sign; covers internet use, prohibited content, personal device use
Rules for personal devices on corp network
MDM enrollment, network segmentation (guest VLAN), data containerisation
Protects confidential info shared with third parties
Vendors, contractors, employees — legal agreement before access
Defines service expectations between provider and customer
Uptime % (e.g., 99.9%), response time, MTTR, remedies for breach
Monitors email, USB, cloud upload for sensitive data (PII, PCI, PHI)
Less binding than SLA — used between internal departments or partners
key_points: SLA 99.9% uptime = ~8.76 hours downtime/year. 99.99% = ~52.6 min/year. 99.999% = ~5.26 min/year.
BYOD risk: personal devices may lack corporate security controls — use network segmentation.
MDM (Mobile Device Management): enforce policies, remote wipe, containerise corp data on personal devices.
PII = Personally Identifiable Information. PHI = Protected Health Information (HIPAA). PCI = Payment Card data.
DLP can be endpoint-based (agent) or network-based (proxy/CASB).

3.4.title: RAID Levels — Quick Reference
rows: None — any disk failure = total loss
Fastest but zero redundancy. Not for important data.
Exact copy on second disk. Usable capacity = 50%.
Most common. Usable = N-1 disks. Slow rebuild.
Safer than RAID 5 for large arrays. Usable = N-2 disks.
key_points: RAID 5: most common for file servers — balance of performance, capacity, fault tolerance. CANNOT survive 2 disk failures.
RAID 6: preferred for large drives (>2TB) where rebuild time increases second failure risk.
RAID 10: best for databases/high I/O — can lose one disk per mirrored pair (possibly multiple).
RAID 0: NEVER for production data — zero fault tolerance.
RAID is NOT a backup — it protects against drive failure, not accidental deletion, ransomware, or site disaster.
Hot spare: idle disk automatically rebuilds when a RAID member fails.

3.4.title: High Availability Concepts
rows: All nodes actively process traffic simultaneously — load balanced
Two web servers both serving requests; traffic split between them
One node active, one on standby — standby takes over on failure
Primary DB server + standby DB; standby activates only on failure
Multiple NICs aggregated into one logical interface
Two 1Gbps NICs bonded = 2Gbps + redundancy; one NIC fails → other carries on
Multiple physical paths to a storage device (SAN)
iSCSI with two HBAs — if one path fails, traffic uses alternate path automatically
Two ISP connections via different paths — if one fails, other carries traffic
System continues at reduced capacity after partial failure
RAID 5 array after 1 disk failure — still operates (degraded) until disk replaced
key_points: Active-Active: all nodes share load → better performance AND redundancy.
Active-Passive: standby wastes resources when idle, but simpler to configure.
NIC teaming modes: Active-Backup (failover only), LACP 802.3ad (active-active + bonding), Round-Robin.
Single point of failure (SPOF): any component whose failure takes down the system — eliminate via redundancy.
Five 9s (99.999%) availability = ~5 minutes downtime/year — requires HA at every layer.
Load balancer: distributes requests to server pool — can do health checks and remove failed servers.

3.5.title: Disaster Recovery Site Types
rows: Just space, power, cooling — NO equipment
Partially equipped — servers present but not fully configured
Fully operational mirror — identical equipment, live data sync
key_points: Hot site: most expensive but fastest failover — data is always current (continuous replication).
Cold site: cheapest — just floor space and power. Requires shipping equipment and full restore.
Warm site: middle ground — hardware present but needs config + data restore.
Cloud DR / DRaaS (Disaster Recovery as a Service): spin up virtual infrastructure in cloud on demand.
Geographic diversity: DR site should be far enough to avoid same regional disaster (hurricane, earthquake).
Test your DR plan regularly — an untested DR plan may fail when needed.

3.5.title: Backup Types Comparison
rows: ALL data regardless of change flag
Only data changed since LAST backup (full OR incremental)
Slowest (need full + all incrementals in sequence)
Full backup + ALL incrementals since full
All data changed since last FULL backup
key_points: Incremental: fast to back up, slow to restore (need full + every incremental in order).
Differential: slower to back up each day (grows), but only need last full + last diff to restore.
3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite.
Backup window: time allowed for backup operation — incrementals fit tighter windows.
Backup rotation schemes: GFS (Grandfather-Father-Son) — daily/weekly/monthly retention tiers.
Test restores regularly — backup files that cannot be restored are worthless.

3.5.title: RTO, RPO, MTTR, MTBF
rows: Maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disaster
Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (how old can the backup be?)
Average time to repair/restore a failed component
Average time between failures of a component or system
key_points: RTO: 'How long can we be down?' — drives DR site choice. RTO=0 → hot site. RTO=days → cold site.
RPO: 'How much data can we lose?' — drives backup frequency. RPO=1hr → backup every hour.
RPO 4 hours + incremental every 4 hours: if disaster strikes, worst case = 4 hours of data lost.
MTBF: used to predict reliability. Higher MTBF = more reliable. Used for redundancy planning.
MTTR: drives support contract choices (4-hour hardware replacement SLA = MTTR ≤ 4 hours).
Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) — increasing MTBF or decreasing MTTR improves availability.
